label: Chapter 5
title: The Cross and the Hill Difficulty

blocks.p: Now I saw in my dream that the highway Christian was to travel was fenced in on both sides by a wall, and the wall was called Salvation. [Isa. 26:1] Up this road, then, burdened Christian ran, but not without great difficulty, because of the load on his back.

He ran like this until he came to a place where the ground rose a little; and on that rise stood a cross, and a little below it, in the hollow, a tomb. So I saw in my dream that just as Christian came up to the cross, his burden came loose from his shoulders and fell off his back, and began to tumble, and kept tumbling until it came to the mouth of the tomb, where it fell in, and I saw it no more.

Then Christian was glad and light of heart, and he said joyfully, “He has given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death.” Then he stood still a while to look and wonder; for it amazed him that the sight of the cross should ease him of his burden like this. So he looked, and looked again, until the springs in his head sent the tears streaming down his cheeks. [Zech. 12:10]

Now as he stood looking and weeping, three Shining Ones came to him and greeted him with “Peace be with you.” The first said to him, “Your sins are forgiven” [Mark 2:5]; the second stripped him of his rags and dressed him in new clothes [Zech. 3:4]; and the third set a mark on his forehead and gave him a scroll with a seal on it, which he told him to look at as he ran, and to hand in at the Celestial Gate. [Eph. 1:13] Then they went their way.

v: Who’s this? The pilgrim. How? It’s very true:
old things have passed away; all’s become new.
Strange! He’s another man, upon my word;
for it’s fine feathers that make a fine bird.

blocks.p: Then Christian gave three leaps for joy, and went on singing:

v: Thus far I came, weighed down with all my sin,
and nothing eased the grief that I was in
until I came here. What a place is this!
Must here be the beginning of my bliss?
Must here the burden tumble from my back?
Must here the cords that bound it to me crack?
Blest cross! Blest tomb! Yet far more blessed be
the Man who there was put to shame for me!

blocks.p: I saw then in my dream that he went on like this until he came down into a hollow, where he saw, a little off the road, three men fast asleep with fetters on their ankles. The name of one was Simple, of another Sloth, and of the third Presumption.

When Christian saw them lying like this, he went to them, in case he might wake them, and called out, “You are like those who sleep on top of a ship’s mast, with the Dead Sea under you, a gulf that has no bottom. [Prov. 23:34] Wake up, then, and come away; and if you are willing, I will help you get your irons off.” He also told them, “If the one who ‘prowls around like a roaring lion’ comes by, you will certainly become a prey to his teeth.” [1 Pet. 5:8]

At that they looked at him, and answered like this. Simple said, “I don’t see any danger.” Sloth said, “Just a little more sleep.” And Presumption said, “Every man must stand on his own two feet. What other answer should I give you?” And so they lay down to sleep again, and Christian went on his way.

Yet it troubled him to think that men in such danger should think so little of the kindness of someone who so freely offered to help them, by waking them, advising them, and offering to help them get their irons off. And as he was troubled about this, he saw two men come tumbling over the wall on the left side of the narrow road, and they hurried up to him. The name of one was Formalist, and the name of the other Hypocrisy. So, as I said, they came up to him, and he began to talk with them.
“Gentlemen, where do you come from, and where are you going?”
“We were born in the land of Vain-glory, and we are going to Mount Zion for praise.”

“Why didn’t you come in at the gate that stands at the beginning of the road? Don’t you know that it is written that whoever does not enter by the door, ‘but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber’?” [John 10:1]
They said that all their countrymen considered going to the gate to get in far too roundabout; and so their usual practice was to take a shortcut and climb over the wall, as they had done.
“But won’t it be counted a trespass against the Lord of the city we’re going to, to defy his revealed will like this?”

They told him he needn’t trouble his head about that; for what they did, they had custom on their side, and could produce, if necessary, witnesses to testify that it had been done for more than a thousand years.
“But,” said Christian, “will your practice stand up in a court of law?”

They told him that a custom of such long standing, more than a thousand years, would no doubt now be accepted as lawful by any impartial judge. “And besides,” they said, “if we get onto the road, what does it matter which way we got in? If we’re in, we’re in. You’re on the road, and as we can see, you came in at the gate; and we’re on the road too, though we came tumbling over the wall. So how is your situation any better than ours?”

“I walk by my Master’s rule; you walk by the crude workings of your own fancies. The Lord of the road already counts you as thieves, so I doubt you’ll be found honest men at the end of it. You came in by yourselves, without his direction; and you will go out by yourselves, without his mercy.”

To this they gave him little answer, except to tell him to look after himself. Then I saw that they all went on, each man on his way, without much conversation with one another; except that these two men told Christian that, as for laws and ordinances, they had no doubt they would keep them as conscientiously as he did. “So,” they said, “we don’t see how you differ from us, except by the coat on your back, which, we suppose, was given to you by some of your neighbors to hide the shame of your nakedness.”

“You will not be saved by laws and ordinances, since you did not come in by the door. [Gal. 2:16] And as for this coat on my back, it was given to me by the Lord of the place I am going to; and, as you say, to cover my nakedness. I take it as a sign of his kindness to me, for I had nothing but rags before. And besides, this comforts me as I go: surely, I think, when I come to the gate of the city, its Lord will recognize me for good, since I have this coat on my back, a coat he gave me freely on the day he stripped me of my rags. Moreover, I have a mark on my forehead, which perhaps you haven’t noticed, which one of my Lord’s closest companions set there on the day my burden fell off my shoulders. I will tell you also that I was given a sealed scroll that day, to comfort me by reading it as I go on the road. I was also told to hand it in at the Celestial Gate, as a pledge that I will surely be let in. All these things, I suspect, you lack; and you lack them because you did not come in at the gate.”

They gave him no answer to these things; they only looked at each other and laughed. Then I saw that they all went on, except that Christian kept ahead and talked to no one but himself, sometimes with sighs and sometimes with comfort. He would also often read in the scroll one of the Shining Ones had given him, and it refreshed him.

Then I saw that they all went on until they came to the foot of the Hill Difficulty, at the bottom of which was a spring. In the same place there were two other roads besides the one that came straight from the gate: one turned to the left and the other to the right at the bottom of the hill; but the narrow road went straight up the hill, and the name of the climb up the side of the hill is Difficulty. Christian now went to the spring and drank from it to refresh himself [Isa. 49:10], and then began to go up the hill, saying:

v: The hill, though high, I’m eager to ascend;
the difficulty will not make me bend;
for I can see the way to life lies here.
Come, take heart now; let’s neither faint nor fear.
Better the right way, though it’s hard to go,
than wrong, though easy, where the end is woe.

blocks.p: The other two also came to the foot of the hill. But when they saw that the hill was steep and high, and that there were two other ways to go, and supposing that these two might meet up again with the road Christian took on the other side of the hill, they decided to take those roads. Now the name of one of these roads was Danger, and the name of the other Destruction. So one of them took the road called Danger, which led him into a great forest; and the other went straight up the road to Destruction, which led him into a wide field full of dark mountains, where he stumbled and fell, and did not rise again.

v: Shall those who start out wrong yet rightly end?
Shall they have safety ever for their friend?
No, no: in headstrong manner they set out,
and headlong they will fall at last, no doubt.

blocks.p: I looked then after Christian, to see him go up the hill, and I saw that he went from running to walking, and from walking to clambering on his hands and knees, because the place was so steep. Now, about halfway to the top of the hill was a pleasant arbor, made by the Lord of the Hill for the refreshment of weary travelers. Christian reached it, and sat down there to rest. Then he pulled his scroll out from the breast of his coat and read it for his comfort. He also began to look over again the coat, or garment, that had been given him as he stood by the cross. Pleasing himself like this for a while, he at last fell into a doze, and then into a deep sleep, which kept him there until it was almost night; and in his sleep his scroll fell out of his hand. Now as he was sleeping, someone came to him and woke him, saying, “Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider her ways and be wise.” [Prov. 6:6] At that Christian jumped up and hurried on his way, and went at a good pace until he came to the top of the hill.
Now, when he had reached the top of the hill, two men came running hard to meet him. The name of one was Timid, and of the other, Mistrust.
“Sirs, what’s the matter?” said Christian. “You’re running the wrong way.”

Timid answered that they had been going to the City of Zion and had got up that difficult place. “But,” he said, “the further we go, the more danger we meet; so we’ve turned around and are going back.”

“Yes,” said Mistrust, “for just ahead of us there are a couple of lions in the road, whether asleep or awake we don’t know; and we couldn’t help thinking that if we came within reach, they would tear us to pieces on the spot.”

“You make me afraid,” said Christian. “But where can I run to be safe? If I go back to my own country, it is ready for fire and brimstone, and I will certainly die there. If I can get to the Celestial City, I am sure to be safe there. I must take the risk. To go back is nothing but death; to go forward is fear of death, and everlasting life beyond it. I will go forward still.”

So Mistrust and Timid ran down the hill, and Christian went on his way. But thinking again about what he had heard from the men, he felt in his coat for his scroll, so that he might read it and be comforted; and he felt, and could not find it. Then Christian was in great distress and did not know what to do; for he had lost the thing that used to relieve him, and that should have been his pass into the Celestial City. He was greatly perplexed and did not know what to do. At last he remembered that he had slept in the arbor on the side of the hill; and falling on his knees, he asked God to forgive him for that foolish act, and then went back to look for his scroll.

But who could ever describe the sorrow in Christian’s heart all the way back? Sometimes he sighed, sometimes he wept, and often he scolded himself for being so foolish as to fall asleep in that place, which was built only for a little refreshment in his weariness. So he went back, looking carefully on this side and that all the way, in hopes he might find the scroll that had so often comforted him on his journey. He went on like this until he came within sight of the arbor where he had sat and slept; but that sight only renewed his sorrow, by bringing his wrong of sleeping fresh to his mind again. [Rev. 2:5; 1 Thess. 5:7-8] So he went on now, grieving over his sinful sleep and saying, “Oh, wretched man that I am, that I should sleep in the daytime! That I should sleep in the middle of difficulty! That I should so indulge the flesh as to use for my body’s ease the resting place the Lord of the Hill built only to relieve the spirits of pilgrims!

“How many steps I’ve taken for nothing! This is what happened to Israel for their sin: they were sent back by the way of the Red Sea. And I am made to tread these steps with sorrow that I might have walked with delight, if it hadn’t been for this sinful sleep. How far along the road I might have been by now! I have to tread these steps three times over when I needed to tread them only once. Yes, and now I’m likely to be caught by the night, for the day is almost gone. Oh, if only I hadn’t slept!”

By this time he had come to the arbor again, and he sat down there for a while and wept. But at last, just as Christian would have wished, he looked sorrowfully under the bench and caught sight of his scroll. Trembling and hurrying, he snatched it up and put it in the breast of his coat. But who can tell how overjoyed this man was when he had got his scroll back! For this scroll was the assurance of his life, and of his acceptance at the haven he longed for. So he tucked it away in his coat, thanked God for directing his eye to the place where it lay, and with joy and tears set out on his journey again. And oh, how nimbly he went up the rest of the hill now!

Yet before he reached the top, the sun went down on Christian; and this made him remember again the folly of his sleeping, and he began to grieve over it once more. “Oh, sinful sleep! Because of you I am likely to be caught by the night on my journey! I must walk without the sun; darkness must cover the path of my feet; and I must hear the noise of the dreadful creatures, all because of my sinful sleep.” [1 Thess. 5:6-7] Now he also remembered the story Mistrust and Timid had told him, of how they were frightened by the sight of the lions. Then Christian said to himself again, “These beasts roam at night for their prey; and if they meet me in the dark, how will I get past them? How will I escape being torn to pieces?”

So he went on his way. But while he was grieving like this over his unhappy blunder, he lifted up his eyes, and there before him was a very stately palace, whose name was Beautiful; and it stood right beside the highway.
